> **Q3: How sensitive is CapRL to the accuracy of QA filtering? What happens if weakly grounded questions are included?**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question regarding the sensitivity of CapRL to the accuracy of QA filtering and the potential impact of weakly grounded data. To address this, we conducted an additional experiment to evaluate the model's performance when training with lower-quality data.
We still used QwenVL-72B to generate QA pairs, and then asked QwenVL-3B to answer the questions both with and without seeing the image. For each question, we shuffled the answer choices and obtained the model answer four times. We filtered out QA pairs for which the accuracy with images was below 75% or the accuracy without images was above 75%. These QA pairs formed the Weakly-Ground-20k set, which we compared against the Strict-Ground-20k set obtained using our original strict filtering. The experimental results are shown below.

| Caption Model | ChartQA | SEED | Info VQA | MMStar | ChartQA Pro | MMMU Pro | MMMU | MathVerse | CharXiv | WeMath | MathVision | Average |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Qwen2.5-VL-3B | 65.6 | 64.1 | 40.2 | 46.4 | 27.1 | 28.6 | 35.1 | 32.8 | 21.8 | 54.4 | 22.6 | 39.9 |
| CapRL-Weak-Ground-20k | 76.3 | 67.2 | 58.1 | 49.5 | 35.9 | 29.6 | 36.2 | 33.5 | 27.1 | 55.3 | 23.4 | 44.7 |
| CapRL-Strict-Ground-20k | 77.1 | 68.1 | 59.6 | 50.8 | 36.9 | 30.0 | 36.5 | 34.8 | 28.3 | 57.7 | 23.4 | 45.7 |

The results indicate that CapRL-Weak-Ground-20k performs noticeably worse than CapRL-Strict-Ground-20k, but still provides a substantial improvement over Qwen2.5-VL-3B. This demonstrates that CapRL is relatively robust to the accuracy of QA filtering, even when the QA quality is lower, our algorithm can still extract useful signals and significantly enhance the capability of Qwen2.5-VL-3B. However, it is important to note that if one aims to obtain the best-performing CapRL model, applying our strict filtering procedure is necessary.

> **Q4: How does CapRL handle creative or abstract images that do not have factual QAs (e.g., artwork, memes)?**

We thank the reviewer for raising this insightful point regarding the handling of non-factual content. For creative or abstract images, such as artwork, the construction of QAs is highly dependent on the specific target task.
For instance, if the objective is to enhance the base model's aesthetic understanding or its ability to describe artistic styles, we can leverage closed-source models or domain-specific models to generate relevant Q&A pairs. By constructing questions such as "Which art movement does this work belong to?" or "What is the overall emotion conveyed by the painting?", we can effectively guide the model to improve its capability in appreciating and describing abstract artistic elements.

> **Q5: Do the authors open CapRL-5M to the community?**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern, which allows us to clarify our plans for release. We are strong advocates for the power of open source and firmly believe that an active community benefits everyone. To that end, we will **release all our training/evaluation code, dataset, and trained models** immediately after the paper is accepted. Our goal is to empower the community to build upon our work in dense image captioning, while also leveraging community feedback to uncover any shortcomings in CapRL and drive its continuous improvement.

Thanks again for your constructive comments and meticulous review, which have helped us significantly improve the paper's quality! Please don't hesitate to let us know if there are any additional clarifications or experiments that we can offer.

> **W3: In the QA curation process, the authors first use QwenVL-72B to generate QA pairs and then QwenVL-3B to verify that the answers are visually grounded and image-dependent. However, this filtering step may remove examples where the smaller model disagrees with the larger one, potentially biasing the dataset toward easier instances (i.e., those correctly answered by the 3B model) and excluding more challenging or informative pairs that only the 72B model answers correctly.**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the overall difficulty of the QA dataset. And we would like to clarify that this design was intentionally adopted to construct QA pairs of appropriate difficulty for the policy model.

To directly evaluate the effect of training on a more challenging QA dataset, we conducted the following experiment. We continued to use QwenVL-72B to generate QA pairs, then filtered out any items that QwenVL-3B could answer correctly by looking only at the question, so as to avoid leakage. After that, we had QwenVL-3B answer the questions with the image, shuffling the options and answering each question four times. We kept only those QA pairs for which QwenVL-3B’s accuracy was below 50%, forming the Difficult-20k set, which we compared against Ori-20k. The results are shown below.


The main reason for this is that for GRPO training, a higher dataset difficulty is not necessarily better. Instead, an appropriate level of difficulty is required for QA (Question Answering) [1,2]. If the difficulty is too high, the rewards across all rollouts will generally be quite low. Consequently, the model will be unable to identify and reward better-performing rollouts, ultimately leading to a decline in model performance. Therefore, the difficulty of the data must be matched to the model's own capabilities when constructing the dataset.

summary.value: This paper proposes CapRL (Captioning Reinforcement Learning), a new framework applying Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to the open-ended image captioning task. CapRL defines caption quality in terms of utility: a caption is good if it enables a non-visual LLM to correctly answer multiple-choice VQA questions about the original image. The method uses an LVLM to generate a caption, and a vision-free LLM to answer questions based solely on that caption, with the resulting accuracy serving as a verifiable binary reward. Then, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is used to train the LVLM with the reward. To support question creation, the authors develop a specific QA curation pipeline to ensure the quality of questions and answers. The authors introduce a large-scale CapRL-5M dataset generated using CapRL-3B, and demonstrate significant improvements across 12 multimodal benchmarks (InfoVQA, ChartQA, SEED, MMStar, etc.), showing performance comparable to much larger models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B).

strengths.value:
The core idea of redefining caption quality through its verifiable downstream utility (i.e., enabling correct VQA responses) is interesting to overcome the long-standing reward-design challenge in open-ended language generation.

The paper is well organized and readable. The methodology is clearly structured, with detailed explanations.

The dataset construction (CapRL-5M) is beneficial to the community if the author makes it open-source.

weaknesses.value:
The two-stage pipeline (multiple QA samples per image, multiple-choice shuffling, etc.) introduces heavy computational overhead.

The reward signal depends entirely on a single non-visual LLM’s comprehension and question-answering ability. If that LLM is weak, biased, or miscalibrated, CapRL may learn suboptimal behaviors.

summary.value: The paper proposes "CapRL," a framework for improving dense image captioning using Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). Instead of relying on subjective human preferences or potentially biased model-based judges, the authors define caption quality by its "utility": a good caption is one that enables a blind LLM to correctly answer visual question-answering (VQA) tasks. This reward signal is used to fine-tune a multimodal model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B). The resulting model is then used to synthesize a large-scale caption dataset. Experiments demonstrate that pretraining on this dataset leads to consistent improvements.

Reviewer Concerns addressed by the rebuttal:

Validity of Proxy Reward (Reviewers ML2d, MPnM): The concern that optimizing for "QA utility" might encourage the model to "game" the system with unnatural captions was addressed by a double-blind human study, where CapRL-3B outperformed the baseline in "Expression Fluency" (4.65 vs 4.55) and "Detail Coverage".

Fairness of Evaluation Methodology (Reviewer UVsw): The concern regarding the disjoint caption-only evaluation was addressed by pointing to the standard pre-training evaluation in Tables 1 and 2, where models pre-trained on CapRL data consistently outperformed baselines (ShareGPT4V, DenseFusion) on 12 downstream benchmarks.

Hallucination Metrics (Reviewer UVsw): The lack of quantitative evidence for hallucination reduction was resolved by providing POPE scores, where CapRL-5M surpassed baselines like Share-1M.

Reviewer Concerns that remains:

Application to Abstract Domains (Reviewer hugc): While the authors proposed qualitative strategies for handling non-factual images via style-based QA, experimental validation for these creative domains remains an area for future work.

> **W6: Answer-model sensitivity: How much do results change when the answer LLM is swapped (different sizes/models)?**

We thank the reviewer for raising this insightful question regarding answer-model sensitivity. To address this concern, we conducted extensive experiments to investigate the impact of different LLM sizes on the CapRL model.
Specifically, we employed the Qwen2.5 series as the answer-model, utilizing five different model sizes ranging from 0.5B to 32B to answer questions based on the captions. The results are summarized in the table below.

| Caption Model | ChartQA | SEED | InfoVQA | MMStar | ChartQAPro | MMMUPro | MMMU | MathVerse | CharXiv | WeMath | MathVision | Average |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Qwen2.5-VL-3B | 65.6 | 64.1 | 40.2 | 46.4 | 27.1 | 28.6 | 35.1 | 32.8 | 21.8 | 54.4 | 22.6 | 39.9 |
| CapRL-3B-20k-Answer0.5b | 74.9 | 66.8 | 54.9 | 48.6 | 33.7 | 30.1 | 35.8 | 34.3 | 24.7 | 56.1 | 23.5 | 43.9 |
| CapRL-3B-20k-Answer1.5b | 76.6 | 67.6 | 59.5 | 50.7 | 36.2 | 29.9 | 36.7 | 35.2 | 26.7 | 56.6 | 23.0 | 45.3 |
| CapRL-3B-20k-Answer3b | 77.1 | 68.1 | 59.6 | 50.8 | 36.9 | 30.0 | 36.5 | 34.8 | 28.3 | 57.7 | 23.4 | 45.7 |

We observed that even when using the smallest 0.5B model, CapRL still yields a significant improvement in the captioning capability of Qwen2.5-VL-3B; however, there is a noticeable performance drop compared to the 3B model. Performance improves marginally from 1.5B to 3B and then begins to saturate, with no significant variance observed between the 7B and 32B models.
These findings indicate that the answer-model does not require excessive parameter size; it simply requires a fundamental capability for information extraction. However, extremely small models, such as the 0.5B variant, appear to lack sufficient capacity for effective extraction.

We have added these quantitative comparisons to Appendix for comprehensive LLM ablation.

> **W1: In Figure 1 of introduction, the authors use the term 'Unified Reward Model as a Judge', but its not exactly clear what this is. Is it an open-source reward model trained to evaluate captionings?**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and for giving us the opportunity to clarify our experimental setting. The term "Unified Reward Model" refers to the work by [1], which is a widely adopted model trained to provide reward signals for both image understanding and image generation tasks. This work has shown that jointly learning to assess multiple tasks may foster a synergistic effect, thereby significantly enhancing the reward model's performance. Due to its remarkable ability to provide rewards, we employed this model to evaluate and reward the quality of captions as a valuable baseline.
We have explicitly added the explanation of "Unified Reward Model as a Judge" in the Introduction to avoid future confusion.

[1] "Unified Reward Model for Multimodal Understanding and Generation", arXiv:2503.05236.

> **W2: In Tables 1 and 2 the authors report results on 12 LVLM benchmarks (InfoVQA, DocVQA, ChartQA, RealWorldQA, MathVista, SEED-Bench 2 Plus, MME, RW MMB, MMStar, MMVet, AI2D, GQA). Could the authors clarify what metric is being reported for each dataset (e.g., accuracy / exact match / task-specific score)? Since the main task in the paper is captioning, it would help to state explicitly how these VQA-style evaluations are computed.**

We appreciate the reviewer raising this important point, which allows us to provide further clarity on our evaluation setting. To address the confusion, we would like to clarify that we do not use the generated captions to directly answer the questions in these VQA benchmarks.
Instead, we evaluate the quality of our caption dataset by integrating it into a standard LVLM training pipeline (Pre-training -> SFT). In our experiments, we substitute the caption dataset(ShareGPT-1M, DenseFusion-1M, and CapRL-1M) used during the pre-training stage  while keeping the subsequent Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stage identical for all models. We then evaluate the resulting LVLMs on general VQA benchmarks (e.g., InfoVQA, DocVQA, ChartQA).

The underlying logic for Tables 1 and 2 is based on the widely established consensus[1,2,3] in LVLM research: higher-quality captions during the pre-training stage lead to superior model performance after consistent SFT. Therefore, the results reported are the performance metrics of the models trained on these datasets, serving as a direct proxy for the quality of the caption data itself.

[1]"ShareGPT4V: Improving Large Multi-Modal Models with Better Captions." arXiv:2311.12793

[2]"LLaVA-OneVision-1.5: Fully Open Framework for Democratized Multimodal Training." arXiv:2509.23661

[3]"DenseFusion-1M: Merging Vision Experts for Comprehensive Multimodal Perception" arXiv:2407.08303

> **W3: When the authors mention Qwen2.5-3B + Qwen2.5-ViT, does this mean Qwen2.5-VL-3B? If not, what is the difference?**

We appreciate the reviewer for seeking clarification on our model architecture. To clarify, "Qwen2.5-3B + Qwen2.5-ViT" is not equivalent to Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Instead, it denotes a specific initialization strategy where we combine Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (a text-pretrained LLM, distinct from the aligned LLM component in Qwen2.5-VL-3B) with the Vision Transformer (ViT) from Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Crucially, the MLP projector connecting them is randomly initialized.

We adopted this setup to strictly simulate a realistic LVLM training scenario. A standard training pipeline typically consists of three stages: Initial Alignment, Further Pre-training, and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). This process necessitates starting with a text-only LLM (which has not yet undergone visual alignment) and a fresh MLP module, rather than using an already fully aligned model like Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

We further clarified these details in the "Implementation Details" part of the Experiment Section.

We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments, careful evaluation, and positive feedback. In response, we have carried out additional experiments and revised the manuscript accordingly. Our point-by-point replies are provided below.

> **W1 & Q2: The two-stage pipeline (multiple QA samples per image, multiple-choice shuffling, etc.) introduces heavy computational overhead.**

We thank the reviewer for raising this important concern regarding computational overhead, as it gives us the opportunity to clarify the actual efficiency of our pipeline.
To address this, we can decompose the training loop of CapRL into three distinct stages: Rollout, Reward Generation (LLM answering QA based on captions), and Training (Optimization). It is important to note that both the Rollout and Training stages are inherent components of any standard RL framework.

|  | Rollout | QA based on caption | Training | total |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CapRL | 51.1s | 6.5s | 58.1s | 115.7s |
| Genaral-RL-Training | 50.5s | 0s | 59.2s | 109.7s |

To rigorously evaluate the time cost, we conducted experiments using 8 GPUs for the Rollout and Training stages, and 2 separate GPUs dedicated to the Reward Generation. As shown in the table, for a single complete RL step, CapRL requires 115.7s, whereas the standard RL baseline requires 109.7s. This represents a marginal increase of only 5.1% in total time.
The additional overhead is incurred solely during the Reward Generation stage, which is computationally inexpensive in our setup. By deploying Qwen2.5-3B on a vLLM server across the 2 dedicated GPUs, the QA process takes only 6.5s per step. This high efficiency is attributed to two main factors:

- Minimal Generation Length: The model is only required to output a single token (the selected option) for each query.

- Inference Acceleration: The use of vLLM significantly speeds up the serving process.

Therefore, the CapRL algorithm introduces only minimal computational overhead.

As shown in the results, while Reasoning-3B-20k achieves a noticeable improvement over Qwen2.5-VL-3B, it falls significantly short of CapRL-3B. Specifically, CapRL-3B surpasses Reasoning-3B-20k by an average of 3.8% across all 11 benchmarks. This substantial margin highlights the superiority of the CapRL algorithm, demonstrating that our method effectively activates the model's captioning capabilities through sparse QA supervision applied directly to the caption.
Furthermore, we observed during training that the Format Reward for Reasoning-3B-20k saturated rapidly, indicating that the model successfully learned to follow the required structure. We attribute its suboptimal performance to the fact that when answering Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs), the model relies primarily on direct visual information from the image rather than the generated caption. Consequently, the QA task fails to provide effective supervision for the captioning process, limiting the improvement of the model's captioning ability.
We have included this experiment in the Appendix to provide a comprehensive comparison.

> **W3: The paper measures caption utility only via MCQs. Does the approach transfer to open-ended QA (and related tasks like grounding or summarization)?**

We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. We fully agree that investigating the transferability of our approach to broader question formats and tasks is a highly promising direction.
Following your advice, we conducted additional experiments on an open-ended QA format. Specifically, we removed the candidate options from all MCQs, transforming them into questions without fixed standard answers. While this significantly increased the difficulty of verifying the model's responses (as simple string matching is no longer viable), we adopted a reliable solution to address this. We employed a two-step strategy: first, the LLM answers the open-ended question based on the generated caption; second, we construct a prompt containing the generated response, the Ground Truth (GT), and the original question, and ask the LLM to judge the correctness of the answer. We found that this "LLM-as-a-judge" strategy effectively resolved the verification challenge. After training with curated 20k Open-ended QA data, we obtained Open-End-QA-20k.

summary.value: This paper proposes the CapRL reframeing the captioning task as “utility for QA.” A caption is good if a vision-free LLM can answer the questions about the image using only that caption. The captioner is trained with RL using this verifiable reward (QA accuracy) in a decoupled two-stage pipeline. They start from a small LVLM (Qwen2.5-VL-3B), optimize it with their RL scheme to get CapRL-3B, and then mass-caption images to create a 5M-caption dataset used in standard three-stage LVLM pretraining.

strengths.value:
- Using QA accuracy as a verifiable signal rather than judge models or reference captions is well-motivated and an interesting way to improve caption quality.
- The proposed approach shows a 3B CapRL-trained captioner matching a **72B** VL model in the decoupled QA-from-caption setting.
- The paper provides useful analyses on (i) training-dataset size, (ii) the number of GRPO generations per step, and (iii) the number of QA pairs per image.

weaknesses.value:
- Could the method incentivize VQA-specific cues rather than balanced, detailed captions? Please report caption quality directly (standard automatic metrics and a small human study) to show quantitative gains.

They utilize the RL-trained model to produce an additional 3M image-caption pairs, which are combined with ShareGPT4V-1M and DenseFusion-1M to form the CapRL-5M dataset. weaknesses.value:
1. While the paper claims that CapRL reduces hallucination, no quantitative evidence is provided for either CapRL-3B or models pretrained on CapRL-1M/5M. The authors are encouraged to report hallucination metrics such as POPE [1] or CHAIR [2] to support this claim.

2. The experiments in Table 3 do not appear to provide a fully fair comparison. The evaluation relies on text-only captions to generate responses, whereas only CapRL has been RL-tuned specifically to produce detailed captions, giving it an inherent advantage. In real-world applications, models are typically used in an end-to-end manner rather than in such a disjoint caption–response setup. Therefore, weaker performance under this prism evaluation does not necessarily indicate poorer downstream capability. I understand the authors’ intention to demonstrate that higher-quality captions can improve downstream QA performance, but a more direct and convincing evaluation would be to apply CapRL as a post-training stage to a VLM and then compare it with other models on these benchmarks under standard end-to-end settings.

However, this filtering step may remove examples where the smaller model disagrees with the larger one, potentially biasing the dataset toward easier instances (i.e., those correctly answered by the 3B model) and excluding more challenging or informative pairs that only the 72B model answers correctly.

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the experimental setup in Table 3. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify the specific objective of this evaluation.

We would like to emphasize that the primary goal of CapRL is to enhance the captioning capabilities of the model. Consequently, all our experiments, including those in Table 1 and Table 3, are designed to assess the quality of captions generated by different models from various perspectives.
In this context, the primary purpose of Table 3 is not to demonstrate that "higher-quality captions improve downstream QA performance". Instead, we treat this relationship as an established premise to benchmark the quality of captions generated by different models. To achieve this, we adopted a pipeline evaluation where captions generated by different models are fed into a fixed Large Language Model (LLM) for Question Answering.

The rationale behind this proxy metric is straightforward: if a generated caption contains fewer hallucinations and provides richer visual details (indicative of high quality), the LLM will naturally achieve higher accuracy. Conversely, if a caption suffers from severe hallucinations or lacks sufficient detail, the LLM's performance will degrade. Therefore, by fixing the answering module (the LLM), this setup allows us to explicitly compare the caption quality produced by the different baselines.

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the alignment between our proxy reward and human-oriented caption quality. We agree that it is crucial to ensure the captions are not merely overfitting to VQA tasks at the expense of readability. To verify whether models trained by CapRL  meet human standards (e.g., fluency, succinctness, informativeness), we conducted extensive validation experiments. Specifically, we performed (1) Human Study and (2) GPT-5 Evaluation. Furthermore, to provide a more comprehensive assessment of overall quality, we also conducted (3) Caption Benchmark Evaluations.

**(1) Human Study**

To further validate these findings, we randomly sampled 200 images from MMStar, ChartQA, InfoVQA, and MMMU, generating captions using Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and CapRL-3B. We invites 9 human judges to evaluate the caption quality based on four criteria: **Detail Coverage, Content Accuracy, Expression Fluency, and Succinctness Degree**. To ensure objectivity, we adhered to a strict double-blind protocol where evaluators were randomly assigned captions without knowledge of the source model. The scores for all four dimensions range from 1 to 5.

| CapRL-3B          | 4.68            | 4.16             | 4.65                | 4.15                 | 4.41 |

As shown in the table, CapRL-3B achieves a much higher average score than Qwen2.5-VL-3B and comparable with Qwen2.5-VL-72B. The improvement is especially prominent in Detail Coverage, demonstrating CapRL-3B’s strong ability to capture fine-grained visual information. The results on Expression Fluency indicate that enhancing caption quality via CapRL does not compromise the model’s linguistic fluency. In addition, CapRL-3B exhibits obvious gains over Qwen2.5-VL-3B in Content Accuracy and Succinctness Degree.

summary.value: The paper proposes CapRL, a reinforcement-learning framework for vision-language models that tackles the problem of reward hacking in open-ended image captioning. Instead of letting a reward model or llm judege directly score captions (which the authors show quickly collapses to trivial, short outputs), CapRL splits evaluation into two stages: (1) use a strong VL model to generate multiple vision-grounded MCQs about an image, and (2) judge a caption by asking a (cheaper) LLM to answer those MCQs using only the caption, averaging over shuffled options to reduce bias. This verifiable reward is then used to RL-tune Qwen2.5-VL variants, and the authors report that the resulting models improve across a wide suite of benchmarks.

strengths.value:
* The idea of evaluating the generated caption, not in terms of the caption itself, but in terms of how well it provides information for downstream QA seems very interesting and novel. 

* More QA data leading to better performance shows the scalability of the method.
